title: Habits: Life on Autopilot. Who Is Really Making Your Decisions?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.
sources: Clear, James, Atomic Habits: An Easy & Proven Way to Build Good Habits & Break Bad Ones, Avery 2018
Jog, Mandar S.; Kubota, Yasuo; Connolly, Christopher I.; Hillegaart, Viveka; Graybiel, Ann M., Building Neural Representations of Habits, “Science” 286 (1999)
Neal, David T.; Wood, Wendy; Wu, Mengju; Kurlander, David, The Pull of the Past: When Do Habits Persist Despite Conflict With Motives?, “Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin” 37 (2011)
Wood, Wendy; Quinn, Jeffrey M.; Kashy, Deborah A., Habits in Everyday Life: Thought, Emotion, and Action, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 83 (2002)
Wood, Wendy; Tam, Leona; Guerrero Witt, Melissa, Changing Circumstances, Disrupting Habits, “Journal of Personality and Social Psychology” 88 (2005)

paragraphs: Wendy Wood and a team of psychologists at the University of Southern California ran an experiment in which moviegoers were handed boxes of popcorn before the film. At random, they received either freshly popped popcorn or popcorn that had been sitting around for a week. People who rarely ate popcorn at the movies ate about half as much of the stale popcorn as of the fresh. Those who were used to having popcorn during a film, however, ate similar amounts of both, even though in a survey they rated the taste of the week-old popcorn just as low as everyone else did. When the same popcorn was served to another group in an ordinary conference room, even people with a strong habit ate about half as much of the stale as of the fresh. So how much they ate was decided more by the place and an ingrained routine than by taste.

A habit is a decision your brain no longer has to make. First you choose consciously and repeat the action, until eventually the place where you usually do something, and the usual time, begin, as it were, to choose for you. Thanks to this mechanism of automation, your attention is free during the day for new and difficult matters. Unfortunately, the same autopilot can lead you just as easily where you want to go as to a place you never planned on. Establishing a new routine like this can take many weeks, and fortunately, missing a single day in the cycle does not wipe out your progress.

The Gospel writer Luke describes the day Jesus returns to Nazareth, where He grew up. Then comes a sentence that is easy to overlook: “As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read…” (Luke 4:16). He had known that room since childhood, because Sabbath after Sabbath He had sat there, first as a boy and later as a young carpenter. That day He reads from the book of Isaiah and announces that the prophecy has just been fulfilled. The most important announcement of His mission is made in the most ordinary place, on the Sabbath, when He would have come to the synagogue anyway. In the same way, Daniel in Babylon knelt three times a day by a window facing Jerusalem. When the day of testing came, Daniel still knelt by the window and prayed as he had before (Daniel 6:10).

Habit alone does not change the heart. Jesus went to the synagogue, where His Father’s Word was heard, and Daniel prayed because he trusted the One he was speaking to. A good plan can help you find a time and a place to meet with God, but it cannot replace a relationship that transforms your life.

Decide today where you will put your Bible tomorrow morning, and where you will put your phone. A small step like this can make it easier to start your day with prayer. And if one morning you skip it, God will not hold it against you. The next day you can simply come back. He will still be there, waiting for you.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: Which of my habits is leading me where I really want to go?
challenge: Before you put your phone down or close your computer, recall one thing you did today without thinking. Consider what set it off: a place, a time of day, a feeling, or the sight of a particular object? Tell God plainly which of your daily habits you would like to hand over to Him.

paragraphs: Week-old popcorn is rubbery and tastes like cardboard, so hardly anyone would enjoy eating it. Yet this is exactly the popcorn that psychologists at the University of Southern California used in a study whose results were published in 2011. In the campus movie theater, just before an ordinary screening, 98 viewers were given boxes of popcorn: at random, some got fresh popcorn, popped an hour earlier, and others stale popcorn, seven days old. Once the lights went down, they watched six movie trailers for 15 minutes, and right after the last one the researchers collected the boxes and checked what proportion of the contents each viewer had eaten.

The result was telling: people who rarely ate popcorn at the movies ate about half as much of the stale popcorn as of the fresh. Viewers who were used to eating popcorn during a film, on the other hand, ate similar amounts of both kinds, about two-thirds of a portion. A survey after the screening showed that participants rated the taste of the stale popcorn much lower than the fresh, regardless of how strong their habit was. So the regulars could tell it tasted bad, and yet their hands kept traveling to the box.

A separate group of 60 people was invited into a conference room that had been darkened just like the movie theater. Participants received either fresh popcorn or popcorn made seven days earlier. This time, instead of trailers, they watched music videos. Under these conditions, even people with a strong habit of eating popcorn at the movies ate much less of it when it was stale.

In another experiment, the researchers told viewers which hand to eat the popcorn with. People with a strong movie-popcorn habit who used their dominant hand ate similar amounts of fresh and stale popcorn. Those eating with their non-dominant hand, by contrast, reached less often for the poor-quality snack. Changing the place or the hand meant that how much popcorn people ate once again depended on how it tasted.

So who was actually making the decision? The taste buds lost out to the surroundings: the darkened room, the soft seat, the big screen. Doesn’t a good part of our everyday life look much the same? How many of our choices are shaped by the places and circumstances we find ourselves in?

sections.heading: A Day on Autopilot
paragraphs: A habit is a decision the brain has stopped making, though it once made it quite consciously. First you chose, then you repeated, until eventually the place and the time began to choose for you.

You put down your keys, switch on the kettle, wash the dishes, and you don’t even notice that you are doing it almost automatically. In your mind you may already be at tomorrow’s meeting, or still going back over this morning’s conversation. This is nothing unusual: in a study of everyday behavior, about 40 percent of the actions people performed were judged to be habitual. Habits let us get on with things while our attention is busy elsewhere.

Animal experiments show how the brain changes as an action becomes a habit. In the late 1990s, neuroscientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology trained rats in a T-shaped maze. A tone told them which way to turn, and choosing the right path earned a reward: a piece of chocolate. As the rats learned, the pattern of neuron activity in the striatum, a structure deep in the brain, changed. Once they had mastered the route, after many repetitions, the neurons’ responses to the turn itself grew weaker, while those linked to the start and the end of the route grew stronger. It looked as though the brain was bundling the whole sequence into a single package: the cue set it off and the reward marked its end. This allowed the middle of the run to happen almost automatically.

Mornings often fall into a familiar sequence: alarm, bathroom, kettle, phone in hand. You don’t have to plan each step, so you can give your attention to new and difficult matters. But this convenience comes at a price. A habit can take you to the goal you long for, but it can just as easily steer you where you have no wish to go. It takes no interest in your resolutions, because it responds only to cues from your surroundings.

Familiar surroundings sustain familiar routines. The same time of day, the same room or the same way home can trigger old behavior almost without our noticing. When everyday life changes, after a move, a new job or at the start of a new semester, the old cues lose their power for a while. If the new place resembles the old one, habits easily come back. When it is clearly different, it is easier to try acting the way you really want to. A change like this can be a good opportunity for a fresh start.

sections.heading: A Routine Takes Root Slowly
paragraphs: A popular myth says that a habit forms in twenty-one days. The number comes from a 1960 book by a plastic surgeon who noticed that his patients needed at least three weeks to get used to their altered faces. He did not study habits, and the words “at least” got lost along the way. Even so, the number has settled permanently into popular belief.

Phillippa Lally of University College London looked at how habits form in everyday life. Participants chose a healthy behavior they had not been doing before and linked it to a daily cue, such as a mealtime. It might be eating a piece of fruit, drinking a bottle of water or going for a fifteen-minute run before dinner. For twelve weeks they tried to repeat their chosen behavior every day and rated how automatic it was becoming.

The results were a long way from the popular figure: it usually took about two months, though the results varied enormously. Interestingly, missing a single day did not noticeably disrupt the process of building the habit. So you don’t always have to start from zero; what matters is getting back into the interrupted pattern at the next opportunity.

James Clear, author of a popular book on habits, adds a sober observation here, however: what counts is the number of repetitions, not simply the passing of time. Someone who did something twice in a month and someone who did it two hundred times lived through the same month. But they built completely different habits.

A few practical tips can be drawn from these studies and observations. It helps to link a new action to an established routine: after your morning tea, read one page of a book; after closing your laptop, stretch for two minutes. The second tip concerns place. If you want to read in the evening, put the book on your pillow; if you want to spend less time scrolling on your phone, charge it in the kitchen. The third tip concerns scale and may be the least obvious: when building a habit, start with a step so small that it almost seems laughable, and then gradually build on it. At the beginning, consistency is what counts. Ambition can come later.

The same principle works in reverse. An unwanted habit is easiest to weaken by changing the cue that sets it off, or by making the action harder to do. Viewers who had to reach for the popcorn with their other hand suddenly began to notice how it tasted. In the same way, moving an app from your phone’s first screen to the last may mean you open it on reflex less often. Sometimes one extra movement is enough to break the automatic chain and give yourself a moment for a conscious choice.

sections.heading: On the Sabbath, as Usual
paragraphs: The Gospel writer Luke describes the day when Jesus, who has already been teaching in the synagogues of Galilee, returns to His home region. He comes to Nazareth, a small town on the slope of a Galilean hill, where He was brought up. Then comes a sentence that is easy to overlook: “As was His custom, He entered the synagogue on the Sabbath. And when He stood up to read…” (Luke 4:16).

It was probably a modest meeting hall, like many in the villages of Galilee, with benches running along the walls. There the Scriptures were read in Hebrew and then explained in Aramaic, the language of everyday life. Jesus had known this room since childhood, because Sabbath after Sabbath He had sat there, first as a boy and later as a young carpenter. Luke calls going to the synagogue on the Sabbath His custom. A little earlier, he mentions that every year His parents went to Jerusalem for the Feast of the Passover, “according to the custom of the Feast” (Luke 2:41-42). The custom was first a family one, and in time it became His own too, as it does for most of us.

That day, something extraordinary happens in the synagogue. Jesus reads from the scroll of the prophet Isaiah the words about good news for the poor and freedom for the oppressed. Then He rolls up the scroll, sits down and declares that this prophecy has been fulfilled that very day (Luke 4:17-21). The most important announcement of His mission is made in the most ordinary of places, on a day when He would have been there anyway. This great moment came after hundreds of ordinary Sabbaths. His listeners immediately ask whether this is not Joseph’s son (Luke 4:22), because that is exactly how they knew Him: from all those ordinary days.

Luke uses the same phrase once more in the Acts of the Apostles, describing Paul, who in Thessalonica goes into the synagogue “as was his custom” (Acts 17:2). So he writes about Jesus and about Paul in almost identical words, because for both of them regular presence in the synagogue was part of their ministry.

Several centuries earlier, in Babylon, already under the rule of the Medes and Persians, lived Daniel, one of the three highest officials in the state (Daniel 6:2). In the upper room of his house he had a window facing Jerusalem. Three times a day he knelt there and prayed, and when the day of testing came, he did it “just as he had done before” (Daniel 6:10). In a hard moment he did not have to invent faithfulness from scratch; his feet already knew the way to the window.

sections.heading: Habit Is Not Everything
paragraphs: What does this mean for us? First, something about how we were created. We learn by repetition, and the brain’s ability to automate actions is a gift, not a defect. Thanks to it, goodness can become second nature to us, and we don’t have to reinvent it every day.

There is, however, an important boundary that is easy to miss. If everything came down to cues and repetitions, changing your life would be merely a matter of clever technique. But a habit in itself does not change the heart, and a good routine can become an empty shell if it does not lead to an encounter with God. Jesus’ custom made sense because His Father’s Word was heard in the synagogue. Daniel’s prayer mattered because on the other side of that prayer was Someone who listens.

Jesus Himself put it in the picture of a vine: “The one who remains in Me, and I in him, will bear much fruit. For apart from Me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch does not strain to produce fruit. Its task is to hold on to the vine, and the harvest grows out of that connection. Technique can prepare the place and the time, but it is God, whom we meet, who transforms character. That is why it is worth nurturing your relationship with Him by setting aside time every day for His Word and prayer. The change we long for grows out of that relationship like fruit, and even the best-organized daily plan cannot produce it on its own.

One missed day, after which we return to our routine, does not undo the process of building a habit. God does not hold us to account for every morning that went by without prayer. Tomorrow He will be waiting again by the same window. A routine you keep coming back to means more than a streak that has never been broken.

Finally, something about making decisions. Simply gritting your teeth works less well than we usually think. What matters more is a prepared place and a small first step. Today you can already decide where you will put your Bible tomorrow morning, and where you will put your phone. A prepared place will not replace meeting God, but it can help you get there.
Prepared by: Marek Micyk
Content editor: Beata Dutkowska

questions: Which of my habits is leading me where I really want to go?
challenge: **In your thoughts.** Recall one thing you did today without thinking. Consider what set it off: a place, a time of day, a feeling, or the sight of a particular object? Tell God plainly which of your daily habits you would like to hand over to Him.

**In action.** Choose one small habit that will help you meet with God every day, and then link it to something you already do. Write your plan in one sentence: “After…, I will…” For example: “After I put the water on for tea, I will read one psalm.” This evening, prepare the place: put your Bible by the kettle, or move your phone charger from the bedroom to the kitchen. Tomorrow, start with the simplest version of this habit: a minute is enough. And if one day you don’t manage it, simply come back to it the next morning.
